tiles.alt: CHAPTER TWO / Everything I Believe Is False
Three people eat dinner in total silence. / That evening. Dinner. / clink / scrape
Harry: A jiffy or two, she'd said. That was four hours ago.

Through the open front door: a very tall witch in a pointed hat stands on the rainy doorstep. The rain stops just short of her, as if it had been told not to. / Harry opened the door. / McGonagall: Good evening. I understand someone in this house has been asking for an owl.
McGonagall: I'm afraid you'll have to make do with me. Minerva McGonagall, Deputy Headmistress.
Harry: The rain isn't touching you.
McGonagall: Hm? Oh. Force of habit.

The living room: Dad, arms crossed; the tall witch; Mum; and Harry, lecturing. / Harry: Now, just to be clear. If the Professor levitates you, Dad, and you know you haven't been attached to any wires, that's sufficient evidence.
Harry: No turning round afterwards and saying it was a magician's trick. If you feel that way, say so now, and we'll design a different experiment.
Dad: Yes, Harry. / The Professor rolled his eyes.
Harry: And Mum, if it doesn't happen, you admit you were mistaken. No saying magic doesn't work when people are sceptical.
McGonagall, deeply amused, draws her wand. / McGonagall: Is that sufficient, Mr Potter? Shall I go ahead and demonstrate?
Harry: Sufficient? Probably not. But it will help. / Harry: Go ahead, Deputy Headmistress.
McGonagall: Just "Professor" will do.
McGonagall: Wingardium Leviosa.

Dad floats up among his own bookshelves, still holding his book, perfectly blank-faced. / Professor Michael Verres-Evans rose gently into the air, until his head was level with the top shelf of Physical Chemistry.
Harry: Huh. / Dad: Huh.
Dad: All right. You can put me down now.
Harry: That's a bit of an anticlimax. You'd think there'd be some more dramatic mental event associated with updating on an observation of infinitesimal probability—
Mum, the witch, and even Dad were giving him that look again.
Harry: I mean, with finding out that everything I believe is false.
McGonagall: Would you like a further demonstration, Mr Potter?
Harry: You don't have to. We've performed a definitive experiment. / Harry: But…
Harry: What else can you do?
Professor McGonagall turned into a cat.
Where McGonagall stood sits a small tabby cat with spectacle-shaped markings round its eyes. Harry has scrambled backwards over a stack of books and landed hard.
McGonagall: I'm sorry, Mr Potter. I should have warned you. / Though the corners of her lips were twitching upwards.
Harry: YOU CAN'T DO THAT!
McGonagall: It's only a Transfiguration. An Animagus transformation, to be exact.

Harry, arms flailing, has a complete meltdown. / Harry: You turned into a cat! A SMALL cat! You violated Conservation of Energy! / Harry: That's not just an arbitrary rule, it's implied by the form of the quantum Hamiltonian! Rejecting it destroys unitarity and then you get faster-than-light signalling! / Harry: And cats are complicated! What about the neurology? How can you go on thinking using a cat-sized brain?!
McGonagall: Magic.
Harry: Magic isn't enough to do that! You'd have to be a god!
McGonagall: That's the first time I've ever been called that.

Planets, a falling apple, atoms, a brain and a storm of equations swirl down into a dark drain. / A blur came over Harry's vision as his brain began to comprehend what had just broken. / Three thousand years of discovering that the music of the planets was the same tune as a falling apple. That the true laws were universal, with no exceptions anywhere. That the mind was the brain, and the brain was made of neurons.
And then a woman turned into a cat. So much for all that.
Harry: And… and what kind of incantation is Wingardium Leviosa? Who invents the words to these spells, nursery schoolers?
McGonagall: That will do, Mr Potter. / McGonagall: If you wish to learn about magic, I suggest that we finalise the paperwork so that you can go to Hogwarts.
Harry: Right. The March of Reason would just have to start over, that was all. They still had the experimental method. That was the important thing. / Harry: How do I get to Hogwarts, then?
A choked laugh escaped Professor McGonagall, as if extracted from her by tweezers.
Dad: Hold on a moment, Harry. Remember why you haven't been going to school? What about your condition? / McGonagall: His condition? What's this?

A clock diagram: Harry's bedtime creeps two hours later every day, all the way round the dial. / Harry: I don't sleep right. My sleep cycle is twenty-six hours long. I go to sleep two hours later, every day. / 10, 12, 2, 4… all the way round the clock
Harry: That's why I haven't been going to a normal school. / Mum: One of the reasons.
McGonagall: Hmmmm. I can't recall hearing of such a condition. I'll ask Madam Pomfrey… / McGonagall: No. I'm sure this won't be a problem—I'll find a solution in time.
McGonagall: Now. What are these other reasons?

Harry: I am a conscientious objector to child conscription, / Harry: on grounds that I should not have to suffer for a disintegrating school system's failure to provide teachers or study materials of even minimally adequate quality.
Dad: Oh! Is that why you bit a maths teacher in third year?
Harry: SHE DIDN'T KNOW WHAT A LOGARITHM WAS!
Memory: a tiny seven-year-old Harry clamped onto a teacher's ankle beneath a blackboard. / Age seven. / chomp
Mum: Of course. Biting her was a very mature response to that. / Dad: A well-considered policy for addressing the problem of teachers who don't understand logarithms.
Harry: I was seven years old! How long are you going to keep bringing that up?
Mum: I know. You bite one maths teacher, and they never let you forget it, do they?
Harry: There! You see what I have to deal with?
Mum flees out of the back door, so fast she runs out of the panel. / Mum: Excuse me!
McGonagall: There… ah… there is to be no biting of teachers at Hogwarts. Is that quite clear, Mr Potter?
Harry: Fine. I won't bite anyone who doesn't bite me first.
Professor Michael Verres-Evans also had to leave the room briefly upon hearing that.
McGonagall: Well. I think, under the circumstances, I should avoid taking you to buy your school things until a day or two before term begins.
Harry: What? Why? The other children already know magic! I have to start catching up right away!

McGonagall: Rest assured, Mr Potter, Hogwarts is quite capable of teaching the basics. / McGonagall: And I suspect that if I leave you alone for two months with your schoolbooks, even without a wand, I will return to this house to find…

Imagined, in a cloud of smoke: a smoking purple crater, a ruined skyline, and a stampede of zebras on fire. / …a crater billowing purple smoke, a depopulated city surrounding it, and a plague of flaming zebras terrorising what remains of England.
Harry's mother and father nodded in perfect unison.
Harry: MUM! DAD!
Harry: Professor? / Harry: Thank you. For coming. For showing us, instead of just telling us.
Something in her face softened, just for a moment. / McGonagall: Goodnight, Mr Potter.
A tabby cat trots off into the rain. / She stepped out into the rain. / And by the bottom step, there was only a tabby cat, trotting briskly away down the wet street.
That night, Harry holds the letter by candlelight, wide awake. / Harry: Magic is real. / Harry: Which means I'm going to need a lot more books.
To be continued
